newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end mostly flat, 10-year sale weak.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end mostly flat, 10-year sale weak.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed mostly flat in light, rangebound trading after weak demand at the second leg of the Treasury's quarterly refunding auction took a toll on prices, analysts said.
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended flat at 97-11/32. Its yield was at 6.71 percent, unchanged from Tuesday's close.
The Treasury sold $12.0 billion of 10-year notes on Wednesday at an average yield of 6.374 percent. The bid-to-cover ratio was a low 1.90 to one.
Experts said the results were disappointing, mainly because the 10-year issues were well-bid in the secondary market before the auction's deadline at 1300 EST/1800 GMT.

"The secondary market was trading very powerfully ... (But) we didn't have much underwriting from customers here. It was a disappointing underwriting," said John Spinello, a managing director at Merrill Lynch and Co Inc.

Analysts said the poor results of the 10-year sale cast doubt over how willing investors were to bid at the Treasury's $10.0 billion auction of 30-year bonds on Thursday, the last leg of the refunding effort.
"When you get a poor underwriting on an issue that seemed to be very well sponsored in the secondary market, the underlying bid probably is not as strong as the Street thought it was," Spinello said.
"So there will be concern with the bonds coming tomorrow in light of a little turn in psychology," he added.
Analysts said a recent slew of new securities, which included Treasury's first issuance of 10-year inflation-protected notes, has been weighing on the market for some time.

Experts said not even a well bid dollar and a jump of more than 100 points in the Dow Jones Industrial Average on Wednesday had enough power to drag the Treasury market out of its current bearish mood.
"Supply has been weighing on prices here. The market seems to be having a hard time digesting all the new securities," said the head of the Treasury desk at a U.S. investment bank.
The dollar was firm at 1.6872 mark in late trading. The Dow closed up 103.52 at 6,961.63 points.
Analysts noticed some foreign-account bidding at the 10-year sale, but the bulk of the securities was perceived to have been bought by the Wall Street dealer community.
"The Street is probably holding more paper than it would like," said Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.
Can the market expect a distribution sell-off soon?
"That would be the worry: that more paper could be distributed later in the week," Leahey added.
Although acknowledging that players were cautious ahead of the 30-year sale, some analysts said, however, they were still hopeful the new benchmark will be well bid.

"We've seen cases when the 10-year hasn't been a perfect barometer of the 30," said a trader at a primary dealership. "But that's not to say people won't be cautious going into the 30-year sale though," he added.
Market players were also bracing for the release of January retail sales data at 0830 EST/1330 GMT on Thursday. The report was not expected to be market friendly.
In a Reuters survey, analysts saw retail sales up 0.7 percent in January against a 0.6 percent rise in the previous month. The ex-auto number was seen up 0.6 percent.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed flat at 5.01 percent. The six-month bill rate fell three basis points to 5.04 percent. The year bill rate was flat at 5.21 percent.

The two-year note closed down 1/32 at 100-00, yielding 5.87 percent. The five-year note traded unchanged at 100-11/32 to yield 6.17 percent. The ten-year note closed flat at 100-20/32, yielding 6.41 percent.
